response.rationale: R1 is the strongest specific candidate because the raw motor distribution and both peroneal nerve conduction studies localize to a severe peroneal-predominant process, especially progression from preserved conduction to no evoked potential. R4 is the broad peripheral-nerve fallback and accounts better for the more diffuse bilateral and reflex findings, but it is less precise. R2/C2 are imaging findings only and do not explain the late conduction failure; R5 is directly contradicted by normal arteriography; R6 is contradicted by the MRI statement of no significant nerve-root/cord compression; R7 lacks raw evidence for vasculitis; C1 is a correlated lateralized restatement of R1 and is discounted.

rejected.why: append-only completion of R1 adding laterality, with no independent raw evidence; correlated restatement.
append-only completion of R2 adding anatomy; correlates with the same MRI span and adds no diagnostic distinction.
Only supports the initial MRI finding of disc herniation, but that report already states no significant compression and it cannot explain the later conduction failure and diffuse deficits.
Plausible distribution-based alternative but lacks independent plexus-level evidence; its supporting data are also compatible with R1 and the MRI does not show new compression.
The decreased ankle-brachial indices are contradicted by the lower-extremity arteriography showing no significant vascular lesions, so PAD is not strongly supported.
The only disc-compression support is the L5-S1 herniation, but the raw MRI explicitly states no significant nerve-root or cord compression; urgent MRI also showed no new compression compression.
Vasculitic neuropathy is not grounded in raw support; its only raw vascular span is the ankle-brachial index, which is contradicted by normal arteriography rather than confirmed.
